title: Planning how a service business earns and delivers
audience: Owners and new operators of service businesses who are planning how a service will reach clients, be delivered, earn money and keep running before they commit time, equipment or staff.
referencesAtStart: No regulator page is cited in the instruction. General planning and pricing terms come from the business.gov.au pages listed in officialReferences, reworded. Licence, insurance, tax and consumer pricing points have not yet been confirmed.
learningOutcomes: Describe, in one sentence, the customer a service serves, including the need and a group the business can reach.
Explain what a client receives from a service as a result they can check, and identify how the work is delivered and who does it.
Separate costs that rise with each job from costs that stay the same, and calculate the monthly job count needed to cover fixed costs from supplied figures.
Identify at least one dependency in a service model, and set a fallback and a test for it before money is committed.

instruction.heading: Why plan the earning and the delivery together
instruction.body: A service business earns money only when a client pays for work that was delivered properly and on time. Keeping the customer, the work, the money and the risks in separate documents can leave the parts unchecked against each other. This lesson gives you one framework, the five-question service check, to test the whole model before you commit time, equipment or staff. The five questions are: who pays and what do they need; what exactly does the client receive; how is the work delivered and by whom; how does money come in and what does each job cost; and what does the model depend on. Answer them in order, then go back and confirm that each answer agrees with the others. A business plan should set direction, show how goals will be reached, and identify and manage risks, so this model sits inside that larger plan. The check is a thinking tool that exposes gaps. It is not a forecast, and the figures belong in a profit and loss forecast and a cash flow forecast once the logic holds (not confirmed by an official source).

instruction.heading: Question one: who pays, and what do they need
instruction.body: Start by listing the people who could need the service, then narrow the list to a group you can reach and can afford to serve. Describe who might need the service and has the budget for it, then test those assumptions with real enquiries or market research (testing method not confirmed by an official source). Divide the market into smaller groups that buy for different reasons, and look at the age, location and income of each group, what it cares about, and who makes the buying decision. A useful customer description says who the person or household is, what problem they face, who decides, and where they look for a provider. Busy households in one suburb with a pool they do not want to maintain themselves is specific enough to plan around. Everyone who owns property is not. Write the need as one sentence, because every later question depends on it. If you cannot write that sentence, you do not yet know who the customer is.

instruction.heading: Question two: what the client actually receives
instruction.body: The client does not buy your tasks. They buy a result they can see, use or rely on. Describe the result as a change the client will notice at the end of the job, such as a lawn that is cut, edged and cleared of clippings by the time they get home, or a door that opens and locks without force. Then state what is included and what is not, because an unclear scope leaves room for disagreement about what the client was promised. Add any promise that goes with the result, such as an arrival window or a return visit if the result is not met, and promise only what your time and skills can deliver. The result also has to beat the client's alternatives, which may be doing nothing, doing the work themselves or using a cheaper provider. Name the alternative your client is most likely to choose, and state what your service gives them that the alternative does not.

instruction.heading: Question three: how the work is delivered, and by whom
instruction.body: Describe the steps that turn a booking into a finished result. These usually run from the first contact, through booking and scheduling, arrival and the work itself, to a check of the result and the client's sign-off. For each step, write who does it: a named person, a vehicle, a tool, or an outside contractor. Be specific about what a job needs at minimum, because that minimum sets how much work you can sell in a day. Time each step on a trial job, including travel, set-up and pack-down, since desk estimates can leave these out. If one person carries out every step, say so, because that person is also the single point of failure. Where a step needs a licence, a qualification or a supervised trainee, record that requirement beside the step and check it separately, as the safety section explains.

instruction.heading: Question four: how money comes in, and what each job costs
instruction.body: Revenue is the money the business earns before any costs are taken out. Decide the pricing basis for each income source: a fixed price per job, an hourly rate, a regular plan paid in instalments, an add-on sold with the main service, or a call-out fee. A business can have more than one source, but each source needs a basis you can explain. Next, sort every cost into one of two groups. Variable costs rise or fall with the number of jobs, such as consumables, fuel, booking fees and the pay of a helper who is paid per job. Fixed costs stay roughly the same whether you work or not, such as vehicle finance, insurance, software subscriptions, phone plans and premises rent. Business.gov.au defines a fixed cost as a cost that is "not part of producing a good or service" (Key financial terms), so the wording here is a working description and not the official definition. The price of a job less its variable cost is the contribution that job makes towards fixed costs, which this course calls "contribution per job". Divide the monthly fixed costs by the contribution per job, and you have the number of jobs a month the model needs to break even. This break-even formula and the "contribution per job" term are the course's own method, not an official definition: business.gov.au's key financial terms page defines break-even as the point when a business's income equals its expenses, and does not state this formula. Keep that sum on paper, because it shows how the model behaves when work is slow.

instruction.heading: Choosing a pricing basis
instruction.body: There are three broad ways to set a price, which business.gov.au calls cost-plus pricing, going rate pricing and value pricing. Cost-based pricing starts from the total cost of making and supplying the job and adds a mark-up. Competition-based pricing, which the page calls going rate pricing, places your price at or near the market price leader. Value-based pricing bases the price on the value the service gives the client, such as time saved or a risk avoided, and not just on cost. Each approach can fail. A cost-based price that ignores what the client will pay can lose work, and a value-based price that ignores your costs can lose money on every job. Check each price against its variable cost and its share of fixed costs before you publish it, and review prices at least once a year, or whenever costs change. Discounts reduce the contribution, so test whether a discounted job still covers its variable costs and makes a contribution to fixed costs.

instruction.heading: What the model depends on
instruction.body: Every service model rests on a few things the business cannot run without and may not control. Look for four kinds of dependency. People: one trained worker, a key subcontractor, or the owner's own availability. Supplies and tools: one product line, one vehicle, one booking platform or one software provider. Conditions outside your control: weather, seasonal demand, access to client sites, or a change in a rule or a price. Clients: a large share of income from one client or one referral source. For each dependency, write what happens if it fails, how long recovery would take, and what fallback you have. A fallback might be a second subcontractor, a waiting list, a minimum notice period, a materials clause in the quote, or a cash reserve. Where a dependency involves a licence, an insurance cover or a regulated product, record it as open until the authority or insurer that governs it has confirmed the requirement.

instruction.heading: Checking the whole model before money is committed
instruction.body: Read the five answers together. Choose one client group and follow it through the model. Does the result that group wants match the work you deliver? Does the way they find you reach the people who can book? Does the price cover the job and make a contribution to fixed costs? Is there a fallback for each dependency the work relies on? Where a link is missing, name the gap in one sentence. Pick the gap that would hurt most if you were wrong, and set a small, low-cost test for it, such as offering a fixed number of booking slots to a set number of prospective clients and recording how many accept. Set a date to review the result and write the outcome beside the model. Only then decide whether to buy equipment, hire, sign a lease or take on a contract. A test is not proof of demand. It is a way to avoid spending money before you know whether the model holds.

procedure: Write the customer in one sentence that names the group, the situation they are in and the need the service meets.
Write the result the client receives, then list what is included in the scope and what is excluded.
List each step from first contact to client sign-off, and name the person, vehicle or contractor who does each step.
Time a trial job, including travel, set-up and pack-down, and record the minutes for each step.
List every cost, sort it into variable or fixed, and note the amount per job or per month.
Set the pricing basis for each income source, and check that each price covers its variable cost.
Calculate the contribution per job and the number of jobs a month needed to cover fixed costs, and show the arithmetic.
List each dependency, the fallback for it and the estimated cost of that fallback.
Choose the gap that matters most, set a test with a size and a review date, and record the outcome before any purchase, hire or lease.

workedExamples.situation: EXAMPLE, invented numbers, not market rates: an owner plans a mobile pet grooming service in a converted van. The owner charges AUD 90 per visit (invented). Each visit uses AUD 6 of products, AUD 9 of fuel and van running costs, and a AUD 2 booking-platform fee (all invented). Fixed costs are AUD 1,100 for van finance, AUD 150 for insurance, AUD 60 for scheduling software and AUD 40 for a phone plan, a total of AUD 1,350 a month (all invented). The owner expects an average of 12 visits a month in the first months (invented).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Does the model cover its fixed costs at 12 visits a month, how many visits does it need, and what should the owner test before buying the van or hiring anyone?
workedExamples.reasoning: Variable cost per visit is AUD 17 (6 + 9 + 2, invented). The contribution per visit is AUD 73 (90 less 17, invented). Fixed costs of AUD 1,350 divided by AUD 73 is about 18.5, so the model needs 19 visits a month to cover fixed costs (invented figures). At 12 visits the total contribution is AUD 876 (12 x 73, invented), which leaves a shortfall of AUD 474 against fixed costs, so the plan does not hold at the expected volume. The main dependency is the owner: one person does every visit, and one illness cancels a day's bookings. A fallback, such as a relief groomer or a waiting list, has a cost that must be added to the model before it is tested. The test is to offer a fixed number of booking slots to a set number of nearby prospective clients (for example, 30 invented clients over four weeks) and record how many book. The owner should commit to the van finance only if bookings reach the volume the model needs.

workedExamples.situation: EXAMPLE, invented numbers: a sole operator offers a garden refresh for AUD 180 per job (invented). The job uses AUD 70 of mulch bought from one supplier and AUD 12 of fuel (invented). The supplier then raises the mulch price by 15 per cent (invented).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How much does the job contribute before and after the price rise, and what dependency does the model reveal?
workedExamples.reasoning: Before the rise the contribution is AUD 98 (180 less 70 and 12, invented). After a 15 per cent rise the mulch costs AUD 80.50 (invented), and the contribution falls to AUD 87.50 (invented), about 11 per cent lower. The model depends on one supplier whose prices the owner does not control. Fallbacks include getting a quote from a second supplier, adding a materials clause to the quote so that the price moves with the supplier's price, or reviewing the job price. The owner should record the dependency with its effect on the contribution, and should review the job price at least once a year and whenever a supplier's price changes.

equipmentAndPpe: A spreadsheet, or paper and a calculator, for the cost sort and the break-even calculation.
Your working notes from the earlier lesson on defining needs and services, and any enquiry records you already hold.
A timer or phone stopwatch, if you run a trial job for the timing step.
No personal protective equipment is needed for this desk-based lesson. Trial jobs carry the hazards of the work itself, which are covered in the lessons for that service.

commonErrors.error: Describing the customer as everyone who could ever need the service.
commonErrors.prevention: Write one sentence that names a group you can reach, and leave out groups you cannot serve well.

commonErrors.error: Describing the result by effort, such as saying the team cleans thoroughly.
commonErrors.prevention: State what the client can see or use at the end, and name the check that confirms it.

commonErrors.error: Costing only materials and forgetting travel, set-up time, insurance and the owner's own pay.
commonErrors.prevention: Sort every cost into variable or fixed, and include travel and set-up time in the cost per job.

commonErrors.error: Publishing a price that covers the job but makes no contribution to fixed costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Calculate the contribution per job and the jobs needed each month before the price is published.

commonErrors.error: Treating a dependency on one person or one supplier as a minor risk.
commonErrors.prevention: Write a fallback and its cost for every dependency the work relies on.

commonErrors.error: Treating a small test result as proof of demand.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the test size and the result, and review the decision on the set date before buying or hiring.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Some services require a licence, registration, permit or qualification. The requirement varies by state and territory and by service. Check each requirement with the relevant authority. This lesson does not grant any licence, and completing it does not allow you to carry out licensed work.
Confirm the cover for each service with an insurer or broker before the cost is put in the model.
Check with the Australian Taxation Office or a registered tax adviser before deciding whether your prices include or exclude GST.
Check the Australian Consumer Law requirements, which apply in every state and territory (not confirmed by an official source: no URL is cited), before publishing prices.

qualityStandard: The five questions are answered in full sentences, and the customer is named specifically enough to reach through at least one route.
Every cost is sorted into variable or fixed, and each job price is checked against its variable cost.
The monthly break-even job count is calculated from the figures used, with the arithmetic shown.
At least one dependency is named with a fallback, the cost of that fallback, and a test or review date.
Every point still to be checked is flagged, and no licence, insurance or tax point is treated as settled until checked.
documentationEvidence: Dated model with a version number and the owner's name, containing the answers to the five questions.
Cost sheet showing the variable and fixed sort, the contribution per job and the break-even job count.
Trial-job timings for each step, if a trial was run.
Dependency list with each fallback, its cost and the review date.
Test record for the chosen gap, with the sample size, the result and the date reviewed.
summary: A service earns money only when a client who needs the result pays for it and the work is delivered.
Answer the five questions in order, then check that the answers agree with one another.
Sort costs into variable and fixed, then use the contribution per job to find the jobs needed each month.
Name each dependency with a fallback, and test the weakest link before money is committed.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which question should you answer first when planning how a service earns and delivers?
options: Which equipment to buy and which van to lease
Who pays for the service and what they need from it
How many staff to hire and how fast to grow

knowledgeChecks.question: A cost rises each time you attend a job, and the vehicle finance stays the same whether you work or not. How should these two costs be described?
options: Both are variable costs for the whole year
Both are fixed costs for the whole business
The first is variable and the second is fixed

knowledgeChecks.question: A job is priced at AUD 90 with AUD 17 of variable cost, and fixed costs are AUD 1,350 a month (all figures invented for this question). Roughly how many jobs a month does the business need to cover its fixed costs?
Which description best fits a dependency in a service model?
options: A single person, supplier or tool the service cannot run without, with a planned fallback
Any cost that appears on the profit and loss statement and each month's bill
The client's written feedback after each job and the review of each one the team gives
